text:
A suspension bridge supports both its dead load, which is its own immense structural weight, and its live load, the shifting burden of vehicles, pedestrians, and wind, by channeling those forces through a carefully balanced system of tension and compression. The load path begins on the bridge deck, the horizontal roadway that traffic directly crosses. Rather than simply sagging under a passing truck, the deck is engineered as a stiffened steel truss or an aerodynamic box girder. This structural rigidity distributes concentrated weight across a wider section of the roadway, preventing any single point from bearing an overwhelming burden before transferring the downward force to the next link in the chain.

Attached at regular intervals along the deck's edges are vertical steel ropes called suspenders or hanger cables. As gravity pulls the deck downward, these hangers stretch taut, placing them in pure tension. They carry the weight straight upward to the massive main cables draped gracefully across the span. Composed of thousands of tightly spun, high-strength steel wires bound together, these main cables can withstand extraordinary pulling forces. As hundreds of suspenders tug downward along their length, the cumulative vertical weight transforms into an enormous tensile force traveling along the curved cables toward either end of the bridge. Because the deck's weight is distributed relatively evenly across the horizontal span, the main cables naturally assume a parabolic curve, efficiently directing the load upward and outward.

At the peaks of this curve stand the towers, tall structures typically constructed from reinforced concrete or steel. The main cables pass over heavy steel grooves called saddles mounted atop the towers, which spread the concentrated pressure evenly across the supporting structure. Because the cables angle downward on both sides of each tower, the tension pulling along them creates a tremendous downward push on the saddles. At this crucial junction, the primary force shifts from tension to compression. Acting as gigantic columns, the towers absorb this vertical squeeze and drive it straight down into deep foundations, often massive concrete caissons or pilings sunk through water and loose sediment until they rest securely on solid bedrock below.

While the towers carry the downward weight into the earth, the main cables still pull violently inward along the horizontal axis. Left unrestrained, this inward tug would yank the towers over and collapse the entire bridge into the waterway or chasm below. To counter this force, the main cables extend past the towers down to the shore, where their bundled wires splay apart and attach to heavy steel eyebars embedded inside colossal concrete blocks or bolted directly into solid rock cliffs known as anchorages. These anchorages resist the relentless upward and inward pull through sheer mass, ground friction, and deep embedment in the terrain. In this final step, the horizontal tension dissipates safely into the ground. By separating the load into vertical compression routed through the towers and horizontal tension locked into the anchorages, the suspension bridge maintains a continuous equilibrium that enables it to span vast distances.
